prompt:
Write an opinion piece of about 800 words on whether cities should remove minimum parking requirements from their planning rules. Take a side and argue for it.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists. Write mostly medium-length, complete sentences.

text:
Cities should scrap their minimum parking requirements, and they should do it soon. The rules were written with good intentions, but they have quietly shaped American cities into places that serve cars first and people second. Removing them does not ban parking. It simply returns a decision to the people who actually pay for it and use it.

Start with what a minimum parking requirement is. It is a rule, written into the zoning code, that forces every new apartment building, restaurant, shop and office to include a fixed number of off-street spaces. The number is usually derived from manuals that estimate peak demand when parking is free and abundant. Planners have often adopted those figures with little local evidence, and the results can be absurd. A small cafe may be forced to build more space for cars than for customers, and a block of apartments for people who do not own cars may still have to pay for a garage.

The first problem is cost, and it is rarely visible. Structured parking can cost tens of thousands of dollars per space to build, and even a surface lot consumes land that could otherwise hold homes or businesses. Developers do not absorb these costs out of generosity. They pass them on to tenants and buyers through higher rents and prices, which means that a household without a car still subsidizes the parking of its neighbors. This is a regressive arrangement, because lower-income households are the most likely to own fewer cars and the least able to afford the extra expense.

The second problem is that mandates make housing harder to build at all. On a small urban lot, the space required for parking can decide whether a project is feasible. Developers may cut the number of units, abandon the project, or never attempt it in the first place. Many older neighborhoods that people love for their density and charm, with narrow lots and buildings that touch the sidewalk, would be illegal to build today for exactly this reason. In a period when most large cities are short of housing, it is hard to defend a rule that reduces the supply of homes in order to guarantee storage for vehicles.

Critics respond that without requirements, new buildings will flood the streets with parked cars and make neighborhoods miserable. This fear is understandable, but it misreads how markets behave. Developers and lenders care a great deal about whether a building is usable, and they will continue to provide parking wherever tenants and customers demand it. Suburban shopping centers and new apartment complexes in car-dependent areas will keep building plenty of spaces, because their tenants insist on them. What changes is that the amount is set by actual need rather than by a formula, so buildings in walkable neighborhoods can offer less and buildings on highways can offer more.

The evidence from places that have tried reform is encouraging. Buffalo eliminated its citywide requirements in 2017, and Minneapolis, Austin and several other cities have followed in recent years, either fully or in large part. In those places, developers have still built parking when it made sense, and many projects have simply become cheaper or more flexible. No city that has taken this step has descended into chaos. The sky-is-falling predictions that accompany every such proposal have so far not materialized.

There is also a deeper question about what a city is for. Every acre devoted to parking is an acre that does not pay property taxes at the same level as a busy storefront or a row of homes. Parking lots spread destinations apart, which makes walking, cycling and transit less practical and forces even more people into cars. They also worsen stormwater runoff and add to the urban heat that makes summers harder. A city that mandates abundant parking is, in effect, mandating the traffic that it later spends enormous sums trying to relieve.

Removing requirements is not the same as ignoring parking. Cities that care about congested curbs can manage them directly, by pricing on-street spaces according to demand, issuing neighborhood permits where appropriate, or sharing revenue with local residents so they gain from the system. These tools address the real problem, which is scarcity at the curb, more precisely than a blanket mandate on private builders ever could. They also make the cost of parking visible to those who use it, which is the first step toward using it wisely.

Some will say that reform is premature in cities where transit is thin and driving remains the norm. But the point of repeal is that it adapts to local conditions. A developer in a car-oriented district will still build the spaces that tenants expect, and a developer near a train station will be free to build more homes instead. The rule that fits everywhere fits almost nowhere, and the sensible alternative is to let each project respond to its own circumstances.

The deepest objection to minimum parking requirements is that they replace judgment with a formula and charge ordinary people for the mistake. Cities ought to set goals about safety, affordability and livability, and then trust builders and residents to find ways of meeting them. Parking will survive repeal, because people will continue to want it. What will disappear is the pretense that planners can know in advance how many spaces every building needs. That is a modest loss, and the gains in housing, affordability and walkable streets are well worth it.
